## Page 1


EISENSTEIN CIRCLE PACKINGS AND THE EISENPINT SCHMIDT
ARRANGEMENT
JAMES RICKARDS AND KATHERINE E. STANGE
Abstract. The Schmidt arrangement of an imaginary quadratic number field K is the orbit of the extended
real line under PSL(2, OK) as Möbius transformations on the extended complex plane. If K ̸= Q(√−3),
then the resulting set of circles can only intersect tangentially, leading to various classes of integral circle
packings, including Apollonian circle packings. When K = Q(√−3), circles can intersect at angles of
π
3
and 2π
3 , making it unclear how to extract circle packings from the arrangement. The goal of this paper is
to study a modification of the Q(√−3)−Schmidt arrangement called the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement
and associated integral Eisenstein circle packings. In analogy to the study of Apollonian circle packings,
we study the number theory of such packings, including associated families of quadratic forms, show the
Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement is formed of exactly all primitive Eisenstein circle packings, show strong
approximation and classify congruence obstructions, prove a density-one local-global statement, and find
quadratic – but alas no cubic – reciprocity obstructions. Unexpected aspects of the Eisenstein case include
the role of congruence subgroups, the bipartite nature of the packings and reciprocity obstructions, the
coeﬀicients of quadratic obstructions, an abundance of extra symmetry, and the need to use “first-odd”
quadratic forms.
1. Introduction
The K−Schmidt arrangement of an imaginary quadratic number field K is the orbit of the extended real
line bR = R ∪{∞} under the group PSL(2, OK), which creates an arrangement of circles in bC (Figure 1a).
Call an individual circle in this orbit a K−Bianchi circle.
Remarkably, as long as K ̸= Q(√−3), any two K−Bianchi circles can only intersect tangentially, giving
this orbit a packing-like structure ([Sta18b, Proposition 4.4]). Many other intriguing arithmetic properties
hold: the intersection points of any two circles lie in K ([Sta18b, Proposition 4.1]), and the orbit is connected
if and only if OK is Euclidean ([Sta18b, Theorem 7.1]). More general arrangements were also studied in
[Mar24], where an entire family of arrangements was associated to each K (many of which include circles
with non-tangent intersections).
From K−Schmidt arrangements one can define K-Apollonian packings [Sta18a], generalizing integral
Apollonian circle packings (the case of K = Q(i)). Apollonian circle packings (not necessarily integral) have
been around long enough that their origin is murky, but their arithmetic properties have been of interest in
recent years since an investigation of Graham, Lagarias, Mallows, Wilks and Yan [Gra+03]. In particular,
an integral Apollonian circle packing is one in which all the curvatures are integral. It has been shown
that the integers satisfy congruence conditions [Gra+03; Fuc11; Haa+24], and conjectured (the local-to-
global conjecture) that all but finitely many integers obeying these conditions will appear [Gra+03; FS11]. A
density-one subset of such are known to appear [BK14], and recently a thin but infinite set of exceptions were
discovered in many (but not all) packings, under the name reciprocity obstructions [Haa+24]. All integral
Apollonian circle packings can be recovered from the Q(i)−Schmidt arrangement by growing a collection of
circles by tangent neighbours.
However, the original work of [Sta18a] avoids the case K = Q(√−3). In this field, we immediately run
into problems: circles may intersect at angles of π
3 and 2π
3 ! Extracting a sub-arrangement containing only
tangency intersections turns out to be challenging.

A primary goal of this paper is to study a suitable adjustment of the theory for Q(√−3). The basic
circle packing definition via geometric configurations and circle swaps, an Eisenstein circle packing, was
2


## Page 3


originally discovered by Andrew Jensen, Cherry Ng, Evan Oliver and Tyler Schrock as part of an undergrad-
uate/graduate research project held at the University of Colorado, Boulder in the summer of 2015, under
the direction of the second author, but essentially independently rediscovered by the first author, which
lends weight to the belief that this is the “natural” packing hidden in Q(√−3). Oliver went on to write
his undergraduate honors thesis describing them [Oli16]. In particular, the team described the same swap
structure we use, but with reference to a cluster of six circles, instead of the four we use here.
The Eisenstein circle packing will be the suitable replacement of Apollonian circle packings in the Eisen-
stein setting. We will examine the geometry, reduction, and basic number theoretic properties of Eisenstein
circle packings, including a formula for the number of primitive integral packings with a given outer cur-
vature, and a somewhat twisted analogue to the crucial relationship between Apollonian circle packings
and binary quadratic forms. Eisenstein circle packings are examples of superintegral crystallographic circle
packings [KN19, Definitions 2 and 10] (see Remark 8.1 and Figure 17), although the Eisenstein strip packing
does not appear on the list of examples yet known [CCS20; CCS18].

Next, we connect this definition to the Q(√−3)−Schmidt arrangement. We modify the Q(√−3)−Schmidt
arrangement to produce the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement, which assembles all primitive Eisenstein pack-
ings into one picture with only tangential intersections. The Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement was also discov-
ered experimentally by the REU group of 2015, as an orbit of a congruence subgroup. Interestingly, several
interacting scaled, translated and rotated copies of the Eisenpint arrangement lie in the Q(√−3)−Schmidt
3


## Page 4


arrangement. We study these arrangements, generalizing work of [Sta18a] describing how they capture all
integral Eisenstein circle packings.
We end by considering the finer number theoretic properties of Eisenstein circle packings. This includes
(again, in analogy to the story for Apollonian circle packings), determining the bad modulus coming from
strong approximation, as well as considering the local-global conjecture for the curvatures. Similarly to the
Apollonian, octahedral, cubic, square, and triangular circle packings [Haa+24; Shi+25], we find quadratic
reciprocity obstructions. Alas, cubic obstructions elude us.
In the remainder of the introduction we provide the main definitions and statements, while proofs and
further details follow in later sections.
1.1. Eisenstein circle packings. An oriented circle in bC := C ∪{∞} is a circle or straight line with an
orientation, where the region to the left is designated as the interior. Oriented circles can be represented as
column vectors (u, v, p, q) ∈R4, where u is the curvature, v is the co-curvature, and p + qi is the curvature-
centre (see Section 2.1). The notion of inversive distance between two oriented circles extends to a symmetric
bilinear form ⟨, ⟩on R4 (Definition 2.3), where a vector C ∈R4 is an oriented circle if and only if ⟨C, C⟩= 1.
Crucially, if C1 and C2 are oriented circles whose exteriors contain ∞, then ⟨C1, C2⟩≤−1 if and only if their
interiors are disjoint. Equality with −1 is equivalent to them being externally tangent.
Definition 1.1. A 4-wheel is 4-tuple W = (C1, C2, C3, C4) of oriented circles such that

The matrix Inv(C1, C2, C3, C4) is called the inversive matrix of our tuple of circles. We sometimes consider
the tuple W itself as a 4 × 4 matrix, where the columns represent the circles as column vectors in R4.
These circles have disjoint interiors and form a tangency cycle in the order C1 →C2 →C3 →C4 →C1.
Call C1 and C3 opposite circles, as well as C2 and C4.
Up to Möbius symmetry and complex conjugation, there is only one 4-wheel.
Proposition 1.2. Given two 4-wheels W and W ′, there exists a Möbius map taking W to either W ′ or the
image of W ′ upon complex conjugation.
The bilinear form ⟨, ⟩gives rise to circle swaps, which build out a circle packing, analogously to Apollonian
circle packings.
Definition 1.3. Given a 4-wheel W = (C1, C2, C3, C4), there are four circle swaps. To construct the ith swap,
consider the circle C′ that is orthogonal to the other three circles in the wheel (besides Ci). The image of
Ci upon inversion through C′ gives C′

swaps.

besides Ci, this implies that replacing Ci with C′

Definition 1.5. An Eisenstein circle packing is a collection E of (oriented) circles in bC obtained by the
following process:
• Start with a 4-wheel W;
• Apply all four circle swaps to W, creating new 4-wheels, and add these new circles to the collection;
• Repeat the process with any new 4-wheels, ad infinitum.
Call the packing integral if all curvatures are integral, and primitive if they additionally share no common
factor.
See Figure 2 for an example of a primitive Eisenstein circle packing, where circles are labeled by curvature.
To describe the geometry of an Eisenstein circle packing, the data beyond the curvatures is extraneous.
Definition 1.6. Any quadruple (a, b, c, d) ∈R4 that satisfies the Eisenstein equation,
(1.1.1)
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 2(a + c)(b + d),
a + b + c + d > 0,
is called an Eisenstein quadruple. If a, b, c, d ∈Z have no common divisor, we call it a primitive Eisenstein
quadruple.
Eisenstein quadruples biject with 4-wheels up to symmetry.
Proposition 1.7. Consider a 4-wheel (C1, C2, C3, C4) where the circles have respective curvatures a, b, c, d.
Then (a, b, c, d) is an Eisenstein quadruple.
Furthermore, given any Eisenstein quadruple, there exists a 4-wheel with those respective curvatures. This
configuration is unique up to translation, rotation, and reflection.
We will restrict our study to Eisenstein quadruples. Considering them as row vectors, the swaps act in
the same fashion, via right multiplication by Si.
Definition 1.8. The Eisenstein swap group is E := ⟨S1, S2, S3, S4⟩≤GL(4, Z).
The four generators have order 2, but do not generate a free group, since the pairs (S1, S3) commute, as
well as (S2, S4). In fact, these are the only relations.
Proposition 1.9. The Eisenstein swap group E is isomorphic to
⟨a, b, c, d | aca−1c−1, bdb−1d−1, a2, b2, c2, d2⟩.

Going back to Eisenstein quadruples, the four circle swaps have the following effect on curvatures:
S1 : (a, b, c, d) →(2b + 2d −a, b, c, d),
S2 : (a, b, c, d) →(a, 2a + 2c −b, c, d),
S3 : (a, b, c, d) →(a, b, 2b + 2d −c, d),
S4 : (a, b, c, d) →(a, b, c, 2a + 2c −d).
The multiset of quadruples formed by iterating the swaps from an initial quadruple q (as row vector)
is given by the orbit qE, and it consists of all 4-wheels in the entire Eisenstein circle packing described in
Definition 1.5.
Definition 1.10. Call any quadruple reachable from q via a series of circle swaps equivalent to q.
In Section 3.4, we develop the reduction theory for Eisenstein quadruples. The main definition and results
are as follows.
Definition 1.11. An Eisenstein quadruple (a, b, c, d) is called reduced if none of the four swaps decrease the
sum a + b + c + d.
Proposition 1.12. Let q be an Eisenstein quadruple. Then, there is at most one reduced quadruple equivalent
to q. If q is integral, there is exactly one.
Three of the smallest curvatures are described by a reduced quadruple.
Proposition 1.13. Let (a, b, c, d) be a reduced Eisenstein quadruple, and assume that a = min{a, b, c, d}.
Then, a ≤0, and the three smallest curvatures in the packing are a, b, d.
As evidenced by Figure 2, curvature c need not be one of the four smallest curvatures.
1.2. Primitive Eisenstein circle packings.
Definition 1.14. A primitive Eisenstein quadruple (a, b, c, d) is in standard position if a ≡b (mod 2) and
c ≡d (mod 2).
By possibly swapping (b, d), every primitive quadruple can be put into standard position. This gives us a
unique way of identifying primitive circle packings.
Proposition 1.15. Every primitive Eisenstein packing corresponds to a unique reduced quadruple (a, b, c, d)
in standard position with a ≤0. This is called the root quadruple of the packing.
Analogously to Apollonian circle packings, there exists a bijection between primitive Eisenstein circle
packings and certain classes of quadratic forms (Section 5). This enables eﬀicient computation of all primitive
Eisenstein packings containing a circle of curvature n, as well as a formula for the total count.

1.3. The Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement. Before investigating the local-global conjecture, we go back
to the Q(√−3)−Schmidt arrangement, adjust it suitably, and verify that this gives rise to (scaled) primitive
Eisenstein circle packings.
Recall that general K−Apollonian packings are constructed in a “greedy” manner: start with one circle
in the K−Schmidt arrangement, adjoin the largest externally tangent circle at each tangency point (i.e. the
immediately tangent circle), and repeat (see [Sta18a, Definition 4.7]).
When K = Q(√−3), we can still attempt this process, as it is not disrupted by the presence of non-tangent
circles. However, this too fails: you can follow paths of immediate tangencies that loop back on themselves
to intersect non-tangentially! This is demonstrated in Figure 4.
Figure 4. Part of the full Schmidt arrangement for K = Q(√−3) (curvatures at most
20). Both red circles are immediately tangent to the blue circle, yet the red circles intersect
non-tangentially.
The root cause is the presence of extra units. Let ω = 1+√−3

the maximal order of Q(√−3). The Schmidt arrangement naturally has a translation by Z[ω] symmetry,
but these units also give rise to rotations by 2π

Thus, in order to extract a reasonable analogue of other K−Schmidt arrangements, one should attempt to
remove these extra symmetries. To this end, take ΓE to be the matrices of PSL(2, Z[ω]) which, modulo 2,
have unit diagonal and are lower triangular, i.e.
ΓE := {M ∈PSL(2, Z[ω]) : M ≡( 1 0

Roughly speaking, Theorem 1.18 shows that we can recover the full Q(√−3)−Schmidt arrangement
through basic rigid motions of the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement.
At last, we can demonstrate that the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement describes all primitive Eisenstein
circle packings. In particular, this prescribes a unique (up to symmetry) placement and orientation in bC for
every primitive Eisenstein circle packing.
Definition 1.19. A collection of circles P straddles a circle C if it intersects both the interior and exterior
of C. We call P tangency-connected if the graph of tangencies is connected. An Eisenpint tangency packing is
a maximal tangency-connected subset P of oriented circles from b such that P does not straddle any circle
in b, and the interiors of P are disjoint.
It is clear from the definition that Eisenpint tangency packings are obtained by picking any circle in b,
greedily adding the immediate tangency circles, and repeating the process ad infinitum. In particular, every
circle in
is a part of exactly two packings: one per orientation.
Symmetries of the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement imply some repetition of packings.
Definition 1.20. Declare two Eisenpint tangency packings as equivalent if they are related by a sequence
of translations by 2Z[ω], rotations by π about the origin, and reflections across the imaginary axis.
These equivalences give rise to the bijection with primitive Eisenstein circle packings, thereby providing
a canonical (up to the above equivalence) way of placing a primitive Eisenstein circle packing in the plane.

1.4. Local-global aspects of primitive Eisenstein circle packings. The tangency graph of an Eisen-
stein circle packing is bipartite (see Figure 5).
Definition 1.22. Call each of the bipartite halves a moiety2 of the packing.
Considering the packing as generated by a 4-wheel (or Eisenstein quadruple) and circle swaps, one moiety
corresponds to the circles which appear in either the first or third position, and the other is the circles
appearing in the second or fourth positions.
We will study the sets of curvatures of the circles in each moiety of the packing separately. This also
makes sense from a thin group point of view: the multiset of curvatures in the whole packing is a union
of four linear functionals on (a, b, c, d) · E: one for each index of the vector. By studying a moiety, we are
only unioning two of these at a time, which reveals certain interesting behaviours that get washed out upon
combining them. It would be reasonable to go one step further and study each index independently, however,
this is unnecessary. Indeed, in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing in standard position, a −c ≡b −d ≡1
(mod 2), so the a−orbit and c−orbit (and b−orbit and d−orbit) are disjoint.
2“Moiety” means one of two halves of a whole, from the french moitié.

Definition 1.23. Let S be a subset of the circles in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing. Denote by c(S)
the multiset of curvatures found in S.
As with Apollonian circle packings, the curvatures have modular restrictions. This time, they occur modulo
4.
Proposition 1.24. Let E be either all or a moiety of the circles in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing.
Then, the set c(E) (mod 4) is either {0, 1, 2} or {0, 2, 3}. In particular, this set is identified by whether the
odd curvatures are all 1 (mod 4) or all 3 (mod 4).
This modular behaviour is captured by the type of the packing or moiety.
Definition 1.25. The type of E is defined by

Any positive integer n equivalent modulo 4 to an element of c(E) (mod 4) is deemed admissible.
Analogously to the Apollonian setting (from [Haa+24]), type (a, b) denotes that there are a residues
modulo 4, with b being the smallest one coprime to 4. The type of one moiety of a packing is equal to the
type of the other: the type is well-defined on the whole packing.
We may ask if the analogue of the local-global conjecture is true for primitive Eisenstein circle packings:
must every suﬀiciently large admissible integer occur in the packing?
To begin, we apply the results of [FSZ19] to conclude that a density one local-to-global statement holds
for Eisenstein packings. This requires an analysis of the strong approximation of a subgroup of SL(2, Z[ω])
governing the packing. The group we define here differs slightly from the groups already used to describe
the packing, because the machinery of [FSZ19] has certain restrictions. In particular, it is a Kleinian group
whose orbit on a collection of circles tangent to the real line gives the Eisenstein strip packing. This is in
contrast to the abstract swap group, which acts on quadruples of circles or curvatures. To be precise, we
define
T : z 7→z + 2,
S : z 7→z/(z + 1),
V : z 7→−z + 1 +

and
E′ := ⟨S, T, V ⟩,
E′′ := E′ ∩SL(2, Z[w]]).
The following is an introductory version of Proposition 8.3.
Proposition 1.26. The circles of the Eisenstein strip packing are made up of two orbits of E′ or four orbits
of E′′.
We prove that E′′ has strong approximation, and as a consequence derive a density one local-to-global
statement.
Theorem 1.27. Any primitive Eisenstein circle packing or a moiety of such satisfies a finite congruence
condition and has a density one set of curvatures amongst the curvatures allowed by its type.
The finite congruence condition given by the analysis is modulo 16. However, it turns out that the set of
admissible curvatures always descends down to modulo 4, giving the type as above (see Remark 4.3).
Despite Theorem 1.27, the local-global conjecture does not hold. To this end, we define the χ2 function
on any circle in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing.

This gives a well-defined invariant on each moiety!
Proposition 1.29. Let E be a primitive Eisenstein circle packing, which divides into moieties E1 ∪E2.
Then, the function χ2 is well-defined on all circles, and constant on each moiety E1 and E2, giving a well
defined notion of χ2(E1) and χ2(E2). If E has type (3, 1), then χ2(E1) = χ2(E2), hence χ2 is well-defined
on the entire packing. If E has type (3, 3), then χ2(E1) = −χ2(E2), hence χ2 alternates across tangencies.
A packing of type (3, 3) with alternating χ2 values is demonstrated in Figure 5.

Figure 5. Circles in the Eisenstein circle packing with root quadruple (−4, 12, 19, 7). The
4718 circles with curvature at most 3000 are shown. Circles in green have χ2 = 1, and circles
in blue have χ2 = −1. These are the two moieties of this packing.
By incorporating the value of χ2 into the type, we get an extended type of a moiety.
Definition 1.30. Let E be a moiety of a packing of type (3, t). The extended type of E is the triple
(3, t, χ2(E)). If t = 1, then this extends to an extended type for the whole packing.
We can now fully state the reciprocity obstructions for half packings.
Theorem 1.31. Let E be a moiety of a primitive Eisenstein circle packing. Then, as long as E does not
have extended type (3, 1, 1), there exists (infinite) quadratic families of admissible curvatures which do not
occur in c(E). A precise description of the families is found in Table 1.
Note that the obstructions in type (3, 3, ±1) are complementary, and thus “wash each other out” when you
pass to the entire primitive Eisenstein circle packing. On the other hand, the obstructions in type (3, 1, −1)
remain in the full packing.

Table 1. Reciprocity obstructions in a moiety of a primitive Eisenstein circle packing.
This behaviour is analogous to the cases studied in [Shi+25]. Only with certain congruence conditions
do they find full reciprocity obstructions for the entire set of circles in octahedral, cubic, triangular, and
square circle packings. However, for each of the four packing types, they still recover partial obstructions
for a moiety of the circles: the patterns of χ2 behave in a predictable way. In future works studying the
local-global question for circle packings, one should be aware of the likely need to partition the set of circles
into two (or more) moieties to obtain finer reciprocity obstructions.
Another point of note is we have reciprocity obstructions of the form 6n2 and 3(2n + 1)2, despite there
being no congruence obstructions at 3. This is in contrast to the previously known examples of reciprocity
obstructions. In the Apollonian case [Haa+24], the reciprocity obstructions are of the form cnk where c is
supported on 2, 3, both of which contribute congruence obstructions as well. Similarly, in the octahedral,
cubic, triangular, and square circle packings studied in [Shi+25], the leading constant in the quadratic
obstructions is only supported at primes where there are congruence obstructions. See Remark 4.10 for
more.
1.5. Computations. An accompanying PARI/GP [PAR26] package to explore Eisenstein circle packings
and the Eisenstein Schmidt arrangement is found in [Ric26]. This includes a comprehensive suite of methods
to create circle packings, find all of the circles or curvatures up to a fixed bound, make LaTeX images of the
packings, and much more. Consult the user’s guide in the project for a full listing of the capabilities.
Using this package, we can further investigate the local-global conjecture. First, we estimate the growth
rate.
Conjecture 1.32. Let E be a moiety of a bounded primitive Eisenstein circle packing. Then, the number of
circles of curvature at most N is asymptotic to cEN δ, where cE is a constant depending on E, and δ ≈1.4124
is the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set of the packing.
This predicted growth rate is analogous to Apollonian circle packings (where δ ≈1.3056), as well as more
general thin groups. To estimate δ, we took the packing with root quadruple (−3, 5, 14, 10), computed all
circles of curvature up to 107, and separated this data into 104 bins of length 103. There were 661, 725, 121
curvatures processed, and running an ordinary least squares regression on the data, the estimate δ ≈1.4124
was found, with an R2 coeﬀicient of 0.999999998.
We take into account the quadratic families found in Theorem 1.31 to make an updated local-global
conjecture.
Definition 1.33. Let E be a moiety of a primitive Eisenstein circle packing. Call a positive integer sporadic
if it is admissible in E, does not appear in E, and does not lie in one of the quadratic families described by
Theorem 1.31. Take the set of all sporadic curvatures to be SE, and the set of sporadic curvatures up to N
is SE(N).
We took all 48 primitive Eisenstein circle packings with root quadruple having all entries bounded by 60,
and computed SE(N) for a varying bound N. In each case, we chose an N large enough so that the final
sporadic curvature found was below N/10. An excerpt of this data is displayed in Table 4. In particular, this
suggests that the sporadic sets are finite.
Conjecture 1.34 (Modified local-global conjecture). The set SE is finite.
1.6. Map of the paper. Sections 2-5 describe the basics of Eisenstein circle packings, going through their
geometry, algebra, and number theory, and finally connecting them to quadratic forms. In Section 6 we begin
11


## Page 12


an interlude where we study the full Eisenstein Schmidt arrangement, from which we extract the smaller
Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement. Section 7 connects these two parts, by demonstrating that the Eisenpint
tangency packings are in fact primitive Eisenstein circle packings, i.e. Theorem 1.21. Section 8 settles strong
approximation and density one local-global, and the reciprocity obstructions are explained in Section 9.
Section 10 concludes the paper with explicit computational evidence towards Conjecture 1.34.

2. Eisenstein circle packings: Geometry
We begin by recalling a treatment of inversive geometry through linear algebra, which was pioneered by
Pedoe [Ped57; Ped70].
2.1. Inversive geometry and oriented circles. To any oriented circle C, we can associate u, v ∈R and
w ∈C so that:
C = {X/Y ∈bC : uXX −wY X −wXY + vY Y = 0},
where
• u ∈R is the curvature of C;
• v ∈R is the co-curvature of C;
• w ∈C is the curvature-centre of C.
Observe that swapping the orientation multiplies u, v, w all by −1 simultaneously.
Furthermore, having chosen such u, v, w,
• they satisfy the relation uv = ww −1;
• u ̸= 0 if and only if C is a circle, which has radius
1
|u|;
• u < 0 if and only if ∞is in the interior of C;
• u > 0 if and only if ∞is in the exterior of C;
• if u ̸= 0, then w is the product of u and the centre of C;
• if u = 0, then w is a unit vector pointing from the exterior to the interior, orthogonal to C;
• v is the curvature of C after the Möbius inversion z →1
z.
Definition 2.1. The quadruple associated to an oriented circle is the column vector (u, v, p, q) ∈R4, where
u is the curvature, v is the co-curvature, and w = p + qi is the curvature-centre.
An oriented circle necessarily satisfies the quadratic form −uv+p2+q2 = 1. Conversely, any (u, v, p, q) ∈R4
satisfying −uv + p2 + q2 = 1 gives an oriented circle.
When considering collections of oriented circles, we typically do not want to consider a circle and its
opposite orientation together. With this in mind, we make the following definition.
Definition 2.2. Consider two oriented circles as distinguishable if the corresponding unoriented circles are
distinct.
We recall the inversive distance between two oriented circles (e.g. from [Ped70, Section 40.2]), which is
Möbius invariant. We use a slightly different convention than the classical inversive distance, which is often
defined as the negative or cosine of our choice (for example, see [Cox66]).
Definition 2.3. Consider two oriented circles C1, C2, with associated quadruples (ui, vi, pi, qi). The inversive
distance between them is given by the symmetric bilinear form

Note that ⟨v, v⟩= 1 if and only if v ∈R4 corresponds to an oriented circle. Furthermore, if C1 and C2 are
distinguishable circles, then

• ⟨C1, C2⟩= −1 if and only if the circles are tangent, with the orientations meeting in opposite directions
at the tangency point;
• ⟨C1, C2⟩= 0 if and only if the circles are mutually orthogonal;
• ⟨C1, C2⟩= 1 if and only if the circles are tangent, with the orientations meeting in the same direction
at the tangency point.
If C1, C2 are tangent Euclidean circles with exteriors containing ∞, then ⟨C1, C2⟩= −1 if and only if they are
externally tangent, i.e. have disjoint interiors.
If the curvatures are non-zero, we also have the formula
⟨C1, C2⟩= 1

where d is the distance between the centres.
2.2. Tangency points of circles. The inversive distance is an inner product on R4, where oriented circles
correspond to vectors C with ⟨C, C⟩= 1. We can express points in bC in this framework as well.
Definition 2.4. Let P ∈bC be a point. The quadruple associated to P is
(
(0, 1, 0, 0)
if P = ∞
(1, p2 + q2, p, q)
if P = p + qi .
If we also label this quadruple P, we note that P ̸= 0 and ⟨P, P⟩= 0. In fact, every non-zero vector
v ∈R4 for which ⟨v, v⟩= 0 can be rescaled by R× in a unique way to produce a point.
With this parametrization, a simple computation demonstrates the following.
Proposition 2.5. A point P is on a circle C if and only if ⟨C, P⟩= 0.
From this, we can describe the tangency point of two circles.
Proposition 2.6. Let C1, C2 be distinguishable circles with ⟨C1, C2⟩= −1. Then, the tangency point is
represented by C1 +C2 (that is, the tangency point is represented by the sum of the vectors in R4 representing
the circles).

quadruples q on the right. The equivalence class of q is the orbit qE. The four generators of E have order 2,
but do not generate a free group, since the pairs (S1, S3) commute, as well as (S2, S4).

We visualize the Cayley graph of Epres in Figure 7. Edges are unoriented as our four generators all have
order 2. From this, it is clear how to define a reduced word that links any two elements of Epres.
Definition 3.5. A reduced word for Epres is a word W = Si1Si2 · · · Sik such that for all 1 ≤j ≤k −1,
(i) ij ̸= ij+1;
(ii) if ij = 3, then ij+1 ̸= 1;
(iii) if ij = 4, then ij+1 ̸= 2.
The Cayley graph is comprised of squares, attached at their corners. As we travel along it, if we pass
between adjacent corners of a square, there is a unique shortest way to do so. If we travel to an opposite
corner, there are two possible choices, but items (ii) and (iii) indicate that we always follow S1 then S3, or
S2 then S4. In particular, given two elements M, N ∈Epres, there exists a unique reduced word W for which
MW = N.

to symmetries in the corresponding Eisenstein packing, and must be accounted for.
Definition 3.6. Let q = (a, b, c, d) be an Eisenstein quadruple. Call the action of a swap on q
• decreasing if a + b + c + d decreases;
• stationary if a + b + c + d is unchanged;
• increasing if a + b + c + d increases.

Consider a word W = Si1Si2 · · · Sik ∈Epres acting on q. Denote qSi1Si2 · · · Sij by qj.
Definition 3.7. The word W is said to be a reduced word for q if W is reduced in Epres, and for all
1 ≤j ≤k −1, Sij+1 is not stationary on qj.
Given any q and equivalent q′ (Definition 1.10), there exists a reduced word W for q for which qW = q′.
Indeed, start with a word W ′ ∈Epres with qW ′ = q′, reduce W ′ in Epres, delete any of the stationary swaps,
and repeat. This will eventually terminate, producing the desired reduced word W for q.
The following proposition generalizes this observation, and sets out the rules and structure of quadruple
reduction. Part (iii) is the statement of Proposition 1.12.
Proposition 3.8. Let q be an Eisenstein quadruple. Then,
(i) If q′ is an Eisenstein quadruple equivalent to q, there is a unique reduced word W for q for which
qW = q′;
(ii) Furthermore, if q is reduced, then W contains only increasing swaps;
(iii) There is at most one reduced quadruple equivalent to q. If q is integral, there is exactly one.
(iv) If q is reduced, then at least one entry of q is non-positive.
In particular, this demonstrates that the stationary swaps account for the only repetition of Eisenstein
quadruples in qEpres. By finding an equivalence class with no stationary swaps (which we will do in the next
section), Proposition 1.9 (that E = Epres) will follow.
Key to Proposition 3.8 is the good behaviour of decreasing/increasing swaps on Eisenstein quadruples
with relation to each other. For example, consider q = (1, 1, −1, −1), which is not an Eisenstein quadruple.
We find that q(S1S3S2S4)2 = q, despite (S1S3S2S4)2 being a non-trivial reduced word for q, contradicting
part (i).

We start the proof with a series of lemmas.
Lemma 3.9. Assume (a, b, c, d) is an Eisenstein quadruple. Then
a + c, b + d > 0,
a + b, a + d, b + c, c + d ≥0.
Proof. Recall the Eisenstein equation,
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 2(a + c)(b + d).
It follows that (a + c)(b + d) ≥0. If equality holds, then a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 0, whence a = b = c = d = 0,
contradiction. Therefore (a + c)(b + d) > 0, so the two factors have the same sign. As a + b + c + d > 0, this
sign is positive.
To finish the claim, by symmetry, it suﬀices to show that a + b < 0 is impossible. If both a < 0 and b < 0,
then 0 < a + c < c and 0 < b + d < d. Thus a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 < 2cd, which rearranges to
a2 + b2 + (c −d)2 < 0,
contradiction. Otherwise, we may assume that a < 0 and b ≥0, and the Eisenstein equation rearranges to
(a + c −d)2 + b2 = 2ab + 2ac + 2bc = 2c(a + b) + 2ab ≤0.
This implies equality with zero, whence b = c = 0 and a = d, so a + b + c + d = 2a > 0, contradiction.
□
Lemma 3.9 implies that there do not exist multiple negative curvatures in a packing, consistent with there
being at most one “outer circle.”
Lemma 3.10. If there exists two swaps that are not increasing, they must be either S1 and S3, or S2 and
S4, with one exception: the V4−orbit of (a, a, 0, 0) for a > 0. In this case, both are stationary.
Note that at least two swaps are increasing from any quadruple.
Proof. Assume otherwise. By applying a V4−permutation, we can assume that S1 and S2 are both decreasing
or stationary. This is equivalent to 2b + 2d −a ≤a and 2a + 2c −b ≤b, hence a ≥b + d and b ≥a + c. By
the Eisenstein equation,
a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 2(a + c)(b + d) ≤2ab,
so (a −b)2 + c2 + d2 ≤0. This is equivalent to a = b and c = d = 0, the sole exception.
□
This lemma is key to the reduction process, as it essentially demonstrates that there is a unique way
to reduce (save for the commuting swaps). In particular, if S = S1 or S3 is increasing for q (hence S is
decreasing for qS), then S2 and S4 are increasing for qS. Similarly, if S = S2 or S4 is increasing for q, then
S1 and S3 are increasing for qS.
Lemma 3.11. There does not exist a non-trivial reduced word W for q for which qW = q.
Proof. Assume otherwise, and across all possible counterexamples (q, W), pick one that minimizes a +
b + c + d (where q = (a, b, c, d)). (Recall that all Eisenstein quadruples have a + b + c + d > 0, so a
minimal counterexample exists.) Note that every quadruple visited in the sequence from q to qW will be a
counterexample (as this is a closed path), so the quadruple sum cannot be smaller than that of q.
Call a S1 or S3 swap a blue swap, and a S2 or S4 swap a red swap. Consider W as broken up into
blocks of blue and red swaps. Each block will have 1 or 2 swaps. The first swap S must be increasing, as
stationary swaps do not occur in reduced words, and a decreasing swap would produce a smaller quadruple
sum counterexample. If the first block has length 2, say SiSj, then Sj must also be increasing. Indeed, since
SiSj = SjSi, the form qSj is also a counterexample to the lemma.
Thus, the first block is only increasing swaps. By Lemma 3.10 (and the subsequent comment), all swaps
in the next block are increasing. This continues inductively, and we see that every swap is increasing, so it
was impossible to end back at q = qW, contradiction.
□

a = b = c = d = 0, contradiction. Part (iv) follows.

Lemma 3.12. Assume that S1 is a stationary swap for q. Then either q or qS3 is reduced. Analogous results

to any Eisenstein quadruple equivalent to q is stationary.
Proof. Stationary swaps correspond to a, c = b + d or b, d = a + c. By Lemma 3.12, any such occurrences
must also occur in the reduced quadruple (the unique one guaranteed by Proposition 3.8(iii)).

4. Eisenstein circle packings: Number Theory
While the congruence obstructions for curvatures will be settled later (Section 8), we will first describe
the behaviour of Eisenstein quadruples modulo 3, 4, and 6.
4.1. Standard position.
Lemma 4.1. Assume (a, b, c, d) is a primitive Eisenstein quadruple. Then exactly one of (a, c) is even, and
exactly one of (b, d) is even.
Proof. From the Eisenstein equation a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 2(a + c)(b + d), it follows that zero, two or four of
a, b, c, d must be even. All four would violate primitivity, and if none were even, then 4 ≡a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ≡
2(a + c)(b + d) ≡0 (mod 8), contradiction. Therefore two are even and two are odd. If a ≡c (mod 2), then
2 ≡a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ≡2(a + c)(b + d) ≡0 (mod 4), contradiction. Thus, it must be that exactly one of
(a, c) is even, and exactly one of (b, d) is even.
□
A consequence of Lemma 4.1 is that every primitive Eisenstein quadruple is either in standard position,
or can be put there by swapping (b, d).
Remark 4.2. Standard position is special to primitive Eisenstein packings, and should not be seen as
“canonical”. It relies on arithmetic data of our curvatures, and since all 4-wheels are Möbius (and conjugation)
equivalent (Proposition 1.2), it is not preserved.
For non-integral packings, if one wanted to choose between (a, b, c, d) and (a, d, c, b), you can make the
choice to take b ≤d. A disadvantage of this with primitive packings will be seen next section, where to
ensure the quadratic forms we construct are primitive and integral, we need to know which of our curvatures
are even and odd. Hence, we stick to standard position.
Another easy result to settle now is Proposition 1.15, which gives a unique representative for each primitive
Eisenstein circle packing.
Proof of Proposition 1.15. Take any Eisenstein quadruple q corresponding to a 4-wheel in a fixed primitive
packing, and Proposition 3.8(iii) gives a unique reduced quadruple (a, b, c, d) in the packing. By part (iv), at
least one entry must be nonpositive. By (possibly) swapping the pair (a, c) with (b, d), and then (possibly)
swapping (a, c), we can ensure that a ≤0.
If a is the only nonpositive curvature, the only ambiguity left is in the swapping of (b, d). This is resolved
by Lemma 4.1, i.e. choosing standard position.
Otherwise, if this quadruple has a second nonpositive curvature, Lemma 3.9 implies that a = 0, as well
as b = 0 or d = 0. Similarly to Lemma 3.10, the quadruple is either (0, 0, b, b) or (0, b, b, 0), and so there is
still no ambiguity other than swapping (b, d), which was already resolved.
□
4.2. Modulo 4. Proposition 1.24 claims that the odd curvatures in a primitive packing are all equivalent
modulo 4. We now settle this claim.
Proof of Proposition 1.24. Let (a, b, c, d) be an Eisenstein quadruple. Using Lemma 4.1, we can put it in
standard position, and further assume that a, b are odd and c, d are even. If we swap c with S3, we find that
2b + 2d −c ≡2(b + d) −c ≡2 −c ≡2 + c
(mod 4),
since b + d is odd and c is even. The analogous result holds for d, hence c, d both represent the two classes
0, 2 (mod 4). On the other hand, we swap a with S1 to get
2b + 2d −a ≡2(b + d) −a ≡2 −a ≡a
(mod 4),
since b + d and a are odd. Thus swapping a does not change it modulo 4, and the same holds for b.

It remains to show that a ≡b (mod 4), hence the modular behaviour on each moiety is identical. We can
rewrite the Eisenstein equation as
(a −b)2 = 2ad + 2bc −(c −d)2.
From above, we can swap c and/or d to a position where c ≡d ≡0 (mod 4), whence 2ad+2bc−(c−d)2 ≡0
(mod 8). Thus 8 | (a −b)2, so a ≡b (mod 4).
□
Remark 4.3. In Theorem 8.9, we confirm that the bad modulus of E′′ (defined before Proposition 1.26) is 16,
hence all congruence obstructions in an orbit must occur modulo 16. In the current section we demonstrated
the stronger result that they in fact occur modulo 4. Indeed, strong approximation is a property of the
entire group E′′, as opposed to an orbit. Orbits of Eisenstein quadruples have restrictions modulo 2, and
these happen to lead to conditions compactly described modulo 4. By contrast, consider (0, 1, 1, 1) · E, where
(0, 1, 1, 1) is not an Eisenstein quadruple modulo 16. By computing the whole orbit, we find that the third
entry is restricted to being 1, 3, 9 (mod 16), which cannot be described modulo a lower power of 2.
4.3. Modulo 3. As the bad modulus for strong approximation is 16, we may expect that nothing interesting
happens modulo 3. Intriguingly, there are modulo 3 solutions that do not lift to modulo 9, and therefore do
not lift to the integers.
Proposition 4.4. Let (a, b, c, d) primitively satisfy the Eisenstein equation modulo 3. Then, up to D8
permutations, we have
(a, b, c, d) ∈{(0, 0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 2, 2), (0, 1, 1, 2), (0, 1, 2, 2), (1, 2, 1, 2)}.
Proof. Recall that x2 ≡0, 1 (mod 3). From the Eisenstein equation a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 = 2(a + c)(b + d), we
analyze how many of a, b, c, d are 0 (mod 3). It cannot be all four, since that would violate primitivity. It
also cannot be three, as the left hand side would be 1 (mod 3) and the right hand side 0 (mod 3).
If it is 2, then we have (a + c)(b + d) ≡1 (mod 3). This leads to the D8 symmetries of the first two
solutions.
If it is 1, then (a + c)(b + d) ≡0 (mod 3), leading to the next two solutions.
Finally, if it is none, then (a + c)(b + d) ≡2 (mod 3), leading to the final solution.
□
By applying circle swaps, we see that (up to symmetry), the first four quadruples in Proposition 4.4 all
lead to each other. On the other hand, the fifth quadruple is preserved under swaps. Tragically, this quadruple
cannot actually lift to the integers, or even modulo 9.
Proposition 4.5. Let (a, b, c, d) primitively satisfy the Eisenstein equation modulo 9. Then at least one of
a, b, c, d is 0 (mod 3). In particular, the solution of (1, 2, 1, 2) (mod 3) does not lift to modulo 9.
Proof. If there were a solution modulo 9 with all curvatures coprime to 3, then from Proposition 4.4 we
could write
a = 1 + 3t,
b = 2 + 3x,
c = 1 + 3y,
d = 2 + 3z.
Plugging this into the Eisenstein equation modulo 9 yields

(mod 9)

(mod 9)

(mod 9),
a contradiction.
□
In particular, there are no obstructions to c(E) (mod 3).
Corollary 4.6. For all primitive Eisenstein circle packings E, we have c(E) (mod 3) = {0, 1, 2}.
Proof. Based on Proposition 4.5, the curvatures of an Eisenstein quadruple must lie in one of the first four
classes (up to symmetry) in Proposition 4.4. After applying circle swaps, these solutions are all in the same
graph, and we always see 0, 1, 2 (mod 3).
□

Corollary 6.16. Let X be a subset of the Eisenstein circles containing only circles from cosets i and j,
where i −j is an edge in Figure 10. Then, circles in X can only intersect tangentially.
Furthermore, if a circle in coset i and a circle in coset j are tangent, either i = j or i −j is an edge in
Figure 10.
Proof. For the first part, assume otherwise. Then there exists circles A, B ∈X that intersect exactly twice.
By Lemma 6.15, ρ2(A) and ρ2(B) intersect exactly twice. However, if they are in the same coset, they
intersect three times, and if they are in opposite cosets, they intersect exactly once, as i −j was an edge.
The second part follows similarly from Lemma 6.15.
□

7. Symmetries of the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement
In order to demonstrate that the Eisenpint Schmidt arrangement produces scaled primitive Eisenstein
circle packings, we must introduce equivalence classes of circles in the arrangement. Recall that b denotes
the set of Eisenpint circles with both orientations. Equivalently, by Proposition 6.6, we can consider integral
coordinates (s, t, x, z) where −3st + x2 −xz + z2 = 1.
The coset of this circle is identified with (s, t, x, z) (mod 2), as in Table 3. Since negation acts trivially
modulo 2, the coset of a circle and its opposite orientation are identical.

it preserves cosets.

Proposition 7.2. The set b is invariant under a rotation by π about the origin.
Proof. This corresponds to the map (s, t, x, z) →(s, t, −x, −z), which clearly preserves the coordinates

□

Proposition 7.3. The set b is invariant under reflection across the imaginary axis.

and only if x ≡0 (mod 2), which occurs in cosets 0 and 4 (as well as 1 and 5, but not the rest).
□

We can now demonstrate that 4-wheels must all be a part of the same maximal tangency packing.
Lemma 7.15. Let (C1, C2, C3, C4) be a 4-wheel with each circle Ci being an Eisenpint circle. Then, the
maximal immediate tangency packing inside b corresponding to C1 contains the entire 4-wheel.
Proof. It suﬀices to show that C2 is in the maximal immediate tangency packing. Assume otherwise: thus,

at most tangential intersections, and therefore satisfy the conditions of Lemma 7.14. In particular, C1, C′, C4
is a triple of Eisenpint circles which are mutually tangent at distinct places, contradicting Lemma 7.13.
□

C.

n=0Rn. Pick any Eisenpint strip
packing circle C, and it suﬀices to show that we can walk via tangencies across only even curvature circles to
reach bR. Pick any 4-wheel containing our starting circle C, and consider reducing this 4-wheel, necessarily
ending up at a cyclic permutation of either (D1, D2, D3, D4) or (D4, D3, D2, D1). Take the union of the circles
we see along the way: of all the 4-wheels in the reduction process. We claim this union contains a tangency
path from C to D1, consisting only of even curvatures (after the starting circle).
They key observation is that in a given 4-wheel with primitive integral curvatures, every circle is tangent
to exactly 1 odd and 1 even curvature circle: this is the content of Lemma 4.1. Now, start a tangency path at
C. We consider step-by-step the 4-wheel reduction process. When we get to a point where we are swapping
out C, then to the tangency path we add the even curvature circle C′ that is tangent to C in the current
4-wheel. This is neither C nor the circle replacing it in the swap. Continue reducing the 4-wheel, and when
we swap out C′, we again extend the tangency path by adding the even curvature circle C′′ that is tangent
to C′ in the current 4-wheel. In this way the last circle in our tangency path is always in the current 4-wheel.
Repeating this procedure, at the very end, we have a tangency path from C to one of D1, D2, D3, D4, where
all curvatures (save possibly the first) are even. If we are at D1 we are done, and otherwise we finally go
from D2 to D1, and are done. This completes the proof that E′(D1) ∪E′(D4) is the Eisenpint strip packing.
The claim for E′′ follows quickly from this. For any word W with an odd number of V ’s, we have W(D1) =
WV (D2) and W(D4) = WV (D3), which implies the result.

Theorem 8.5. The group E′′ satisfies the hypotheses of [FSZ19, Theorem 1.3, 1.6], namely:
(1) it is a Kleinian group contained in PSL(2, Z[ω]);
(2) it contains a congruence subgroup of PSL(2, Z);
(3) it is finitely generated;
(4) the limit set has Hausdorff dimension greater than 1;
(5) it is Zariski dense (in the sense of [FSZ19]);
(6) it has infinite covolume;
(7) it is geometrically finite.
Proof. Parts (1) through (3) are immediate from the definition. Next, [BJ97, Corollary 1.8] implies that
the limit set of a finitely-generated Kleinian group is either totally disconnected, a circle, or of Hausdorff
dimension > 1. The limit set of E′ (hence equivalently E′′) includes bR and other circles, whence it is of
Hausdorff dimension > 1. This verifies (4).
Now we consider Zariski density. The sense in [FSZ19] is to consider PGL(2, C) as a real algebraic group;
that is, use Weil restriction. In this setup, we can move between Kleinian groups and subgroups of the
orthogonal group O3,1 < GL4 via the spin homomorphism SL(2, C) →SO+
3,1(R). In particular, consider the
Zariski closure G of the image of E′′. The possibilities for this group are classified as in the proofs of [Sta18a,
Theorem 9.4] and [Fuc11, Lemma 1.6(ii)]. In particular, since G is not finite and satisfies (4), it is either O3,1
or SO3,1, exactly as in [Sta18a, Theorem 9.4]. Pulling back through the spin map, we find that E′′ is Zariski
dense, i.e. (5).

9. Reciprocity obstructions
We adapt the strategy of [Haa+24], which has also been subsequently used by [Shi+25]. For each circle C,
using the associated quadratic form, we define a symbol χ2(C) = ±1, which governs the reciprocity behaviour
of the curvature with respect to the curvatures of tangent circles. We are then able to prove that this symbol
is either always preserved or always swaps across a coprime tangency. Since the graph of coprime tangencies
is connected and bipartite, this implies that we have a well-defined quadratic invariant on either the whole
packing, or each of the two bipartite halves. In most of these cases, we derive reciprocity obstructions.
9.1. The symbol χ2. For now, forget the definition of χ2 from Definition 1.28. We will recover this expres-
sion later in Proposition 9.6.
Consider a circle C of curvature n in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing, and complete it to an Eisenstein
quadruple in standard position q = (n, b, c, d). This is associated to the primitive first-odd binary quadratic
form ϕ(q)(x, y) = Ax2 + Bxy + Cy2 (Proposition 5.13).

The final piece is the existence of coprime tangency paths between any pairs of circles. In the Apollonian
case ([Haa+24, Corollary 4.7]), given a pair of tangent circles whose curvatures share a non-trivial factor,
we considered the family of circles tangent to both. Their curvatures were values of a quadratic form, and it
was shown that one of them will be coprime to our two original circle curvatures.
In the Eisenstein case, we need a modification, as there are no triples of mutually tangent circles. Instead,
we must follow a procedure similar to [Shi+25], where we pass to at least two auxiliary circles to make a
coprime path. To begin, we require a standard lemma about quadratics.
Lemma 9.8. Let f(x) = Ax2 + Bx + C ∈Z[x]. If p is an odd prime with p ∤gcd(A, B, C), then there exists
a residue r such that if x ≡r (mod p), then p ∤f(x).
Proof. As divisibility by p is preserved across the x (mod p) residue class, it suﬀices to prove that at least
one integer x satisfies f(x) is coprime to p. If not, then p | f(0) = C, p | f(1) = A + B + C, and
p | f(−1) = A −B + C, whence p | A, B, C, contradiction.
□
Next, we make the coprime path, but ignore the prime 2, zero curvature circles, and equal curvature
circles.
Lemma 9.9. Let C and C′ be tangent circles with distinct and non-zero curvatures in a primitive Eisenstein
circle packing. Then, there exist circles C1, C2 in the packing such that
• (C, C1, C2, C′) is a 4-wheel, hence C −C1 −C2 −C′ is a path of tangent circles;
• The curvatures of the four circles are distinct and non-zero;
• In each of the three pairs of consecutive tangent circles (C, C1), (C1, C2), and (C2, C′), their curvatures
share no odd prime factors.

We now define three finite sets of primes:
• P1 is the set of prime divisors of a that do not divide g;
• P2 is the set of prime divisors of d that do not divide g;
• P3 is the set of prime divisors of a −d.
The above computation shows that P1 and P2 are disjoint, and if p ∈P3 ∩(P1 ∪P2), then p | g, contradiction.
Thus, the three sets are disjoint.

• For p ∈P1 ∪P3, if p ̸= 3, then Lemma 9.8 applies with bn. If p = 3, then since p | a or p | a −d, we
must have (a, b0, c0, d0) ̸≡(a, 0, −a, −a) (mod 3), as otherwise the quadruple would not be primitive
at 3. In particular, Lemma 9.8 always applies, and guarantees a residue rp so that if n ≡rp (mod p),
then bn ̸≡0 (mod p).
• For p ∈P2, apply the analogous result with cn, obtaining a residue rp so that if n ≡rp (mod p),
then cn ̸≡0 (mod p).
As our three sets of primes are disjoint, by the Chinese remainder theorem, we can combine the above
residues into one class r (mod N), where N is the product of primes in P1 ∪P2 ∪P3. We claim that any
n ≡r (mod N) will satisfy the odd-coprimality on pairs.
For (a, bn), let p be an odd prime divisor of a. If p | g, then we already know that p ∤bn, hence p ∤gcd(a, bn).
Otherwise, p ∈P1, and by our construction, p ∤bn, so again, p ∤gcd(a, bn), proving that this is a power of 2.
The argument for (cn, d) is analogous, so it remains to check (bn, cn). Let p | bn, cn, and by the Eisenstein
equation, we have
a2 + d2 ≡a2 + b2

(mod p),
whence p | (a −d)2, so p | a −d. Therefore p ∈P3, and by our construction, p ∤bn, so gcd(bn, cn) is a power
of 2, as claimed.
To finish, we just need to note that the n2 coeﬀicient in bn and cn is 2a + 2d, which is non-zero. (Indeed,
otherwise, a = −d ̸= 0, but there is a unique smallest absolute curvature in a bounded packing.) Thus,
for some large n ≡r (mod N), the four curvatures a, bn, cn, d must be distinct and non-zero, the final
requirement.
□
The reason we assumed that our starting circles had non-zero curvature was that otherwise, P1 or P2 would
be infinite. Similarly, if they had equal curvature, then P3 is infinite. First, we rectify the zero curvature
issue.
Lemma 9.10. Let C and C′ be tangent circles in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing, where C has curvature
zero. Then, there is a tangency path between C and C′ where consecutive circles have coprime curvatures.
Proof. Since we have a curvature zero circle, we must be in the Eisenstein strip packing, Figure 16. If C′ is
also of curvature 0, then we can traverse across the two curvature 1 circles in the root 4-wheel of curvatures
(0, 0, 1, 1). Otherwise, assume that (C, C1, C2, C3) is a 4-wheel with curvatures (0, b, c, d). By the Eisenstein
equation, b2 + c2 + d2 ≡2c(b + d). So, if p is a prime that divides either (b, c) or (c, d), then it divides b, c, d,
whence (0, b, c, d) is not primitive, contradiction. Therefore it follows that gcd(b, c) = gcd(c, d) = 1.
Thus, we can pick any 4-wheel (C, C1, C2, C′), and reduce it, eventually obtaining a quadruple of circles
with curvatures being a permutation of (0, 0, 1, 1). However, along the way, start with C′. Any time we are
swapping this circle out, move to the tangent circle C2, which must have coprime curvature. Repeat this
process, obtaining a coprime tangency path from C2 to one of the other circles in the base quadruple. We
can then move directly to C (if curvature 1), or through the two curvature 1 circles to C. In any case, we
have found our tangency-connected path.
□
Finally, we can turn any tangency-connected path into a coprime tangency-connected path.
Proposition 9.11. Let C and C′ be circles in a primitive Eisenstein circle packing. Then, there is a tangency
path between C and C′ where consecutive circles have coprime curvatures.
Proof. The tangency graph is connected, so to begin, pick any path. Consider any consecutive tangency
D −D′ of curvatures d, d′ respectively, where gcd(d, d′) > 1. We claim that we can replace this with a path
D −D1 −D2 −· · · −Dn −D′, where every pair of consecutive circles have coprime curvatures. If this is true,
then repeating this replacement for all such pairs produces the final path.
Assume that d ̸= d′. If either are 0, we are done by Lemma 9.10. Otherwise, by Lemma 9.9, we can find
circles D1 and D2 of curvatures x, y which make a 4-wheel of curvatures (d, x, y, d′), where consecutive pairs
are distinct, non-zero, and share no odd prime divisors. If d and d′ are even, then by Lemma 4.1, x and y
are necessarily odd, whence gcd(d, x) = gcd(x, y) = gcd(y, d′) = 1.
If d and d′ are odd, then x and y are even, so gcd(d, x) = gcd(y, d′) = 1, but gcd(x, y) is an even power
of 2. In this case, we can just repeat the argument for circles D1 and D2, ending up with a 6 circle path
between D and D′.

Similarly, if one of d, d′ is even and the other is odd, we can assume that d is even and d′ is odd. Therefore
x is even and y is odd, so gcd(x, y) = gcd(y, d′) = 1. This time gcd(d, x) is an even power of 2, so repeat the
argument on D and D1 to get a valid 6 circle coprime path between D and D′.
The final case is if d = d′ ̸= 0. Pick a 4-wheel (D, D1, D2, D′), and by alternately applying swaps S2
and S3 some number of times, we can reduce to the case where each pair of consecutive circles has distinct
curvature. Repeat the above arguments for each pair to derive the final result.
□

10. Computational results on sporadic curvatures
There are four extended types possible. For every packing of extended type (3, 1, ±1), we get two moieties:
one for the odd index circles (1 and 3, denoted O), and one for the even index circles (2 and 4, denoted E).
For each packing of type (3, 3), one moiety has extended type (3, 3, 1), and the other moiety has extended
type (3, 3, −1).
58


## Page 59


Overall, for the 48 root quadruples with curvatures at most 60, we have 96 sets of moieties, which divide
into
• 26 of extended type (3, 1, 1) (with two being equal: in the packing (0, 0, 1, 1), the even index and odd
index moieties clearly contain the same sets of curvatures);
• 20 of extended type (3, 1, −1);
• 25 of extended type (3, 3, 1);
• 25 of extended type (3, 3, −1).
For each moiety, we computed the sporadic set SE(N) for N = 108, and observed the final sporadic
curvature found. If it was larger than N/10, we increased N and recomputed. In each such case, we were able
to succeed for some N ≤3 · 1010. A summary of these computations for 4 small packings of each extended
type is found in Table 4. While this does not prove that SE is finite, it is strong evidence towards this
conjecture, and further suggests that we have found the exact sporadic set in the described cases.
